title: That you are
hookLine: a proud son comes home from twelve years of study, his father asks one question, and a line two schools of Hindu thought read two ways
carry: atman and Brahman: one, or two?
tomorrow: the greatest archer alive drops his bow. why?
last: A BOW TO THE DIVINE IN THE OTHER.

lines: DID YOU ASK FOR THE TEACHING?
cards: In the Chandogya Upanishad, a boy named Shvetaketu leaves home at twelve to study the Vedas. He comes back at twenty-four, knowing all of them, and very pleased with himself.
His father, Uddalaka, watches him walk in and asks one question. Did you ask for the teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, and the unknown known? Shvetaketu has no idea what he means.
So the father starts again from the beginning, and his teaching keeps coming back to three words: tat tvam asi. That you are.

teach.h: A LONG A AND A SHORT A MELT.
teach.b: Here's the join. In the text, the line follows the word atma, the self: sa atma, tat tvam asi.

That is the self; that you are. Now, in sandhi, when a long a meets a short a, the two melt into one long a. So atma followed by atat, which means not that, comes out sounding and looking just like atma followed by tat.
And two great schools of Hindu thought split it differently. Shankara's school, Advaita, reads tat: that you are. Your deepest self and Brahman, the ground of everything, are one.
Their best case: the father says it right after examples where the many dissolve into the one, like salt stirred into water, gone from sight but present in every sip.
Madhva's school, Dvaita, offers another split: atat, not that. You are not that. The self and God are truly two, and the self depends on God.
Their best case: the self forgets, suffers and needs grace; the ground of everything doesn't, and the letters allow a reading that keeps the two distinct. And this is no grammar quibble.

teach.h: ATMAN AND BRAHMAN: ONE, OR TWO?
teach.b: It's one of the deepest questions in Vedanta: is your atman, your deepest self, one with Brahman, or forever distinct and held up by God? For Advaita, the self in the stranger is your own.
For Dvaita, everything you have is grace, and the right answer is devotion.

how: Tat tvam asi is studied and debated in Vedanta schools; Advaita teachers read it as the identity of the self and Brahman, and Dvaita teachers in Madhva's line read it in ways that keep the self and God distinct.

o: how a line is chanted at two different speeds
how two schools translate a word differently
whether your deepest self is one with Brahman, or two

games.q: one line, two readings — tap the pairs.
p: the father teaching in the Chandogya
the son who came home proud at twenty-four

s: the written letters settle whether the line says tat or atat
a long a and a short a melt into one long a, so joined letters allow both.
in the Chandogya, the father uses salt dissolved in water
gone from sight but present in every sip.
Hindu thought reads tat tvam asi in only one way
Advaita and Dvaita read it differently, from the same letters.

games.q: at dinner, a friend says the Dvaita reading is just a way to dodge tat tvam asi. you lean toward Advaita. what's Dvaita's best case about the self?
o: the letters allow atat, and a self that forgets and needs grace isn't the same as God.
it isn't really a reading; it's a refusal to read the line at all.
it agrees with Advaita completely, just in different words.
games.why: a long a plus a short a melts into one, so the page allows atat. Dvaita reads the self and God as two; Advaita reads them as one. both read the same letters.

practice: Write tat tvam asi on paper, and under it, atat tvam asi. Look at the two lines side by side for a few slow breaths. Then think of one person you'll see tomorrow.
Try the first line: the same self looking out of their eyes. Then the second: a soul held up by the same God as you. Notice which one changes how you'd treat them.

wordCard.voice: Sandhi plainly: today, a long a and a short a melting into one, so that that, and not that, can look the same, and atman and Brahman can be read as one, or as two.

orig.note: Sanskrit: tat tvam asi, that you are, written joined; Chandogya Upanishad, chapter 6.

carryVoice: Your line: atman and Brahman, one, or two? Shvetaketu's father asked it with three words. Good night.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.1.1–3 (Shvetaketu leaves at twelve, returns at twenty-four proud; Uddalaka asks about the teaching by which the unheard becomes heard)
Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7 and following (sa ātmā tat tvam asi, śvetaketo)
Ashtadhyayi 6.1.101 (akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ: like vowels merge into the long vowel)
Shankara's Chandogya Upanishad commentary (tat tvam asi as identity); Madhva's Chandogya commentary and Dvaita readings (including the split sa ātmā atat tvam asi)
